beats.title: Match the non-included angle
beats.instruction: Drag point F to adjust angle ∠D in △DEF. Make ∠D equal to 53° to match ∠A in △ABC. With ∠B ≅ ∠E and BC ≅ EF (non-included side) already established, matching the second angle completes AAS.
beats.successMessage: Both angle pairs match and BC ≅ EF — AAS confirms △ABC ≅ △DEF!

steps.text: Identify two angle pairs. ∠A = ∠D = 53° and ∠B = ∠E = 90°. Both angle pairs are congruent.
The side BC = EF = 4. Crucially, BC is opposite ∠A and EF is opposite ∠D — this side is NOT between the two known angles (making it AAS, not ASA).
Since ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180° forces ∠C = 37° = ∠F, all three angles match. The third angle theorem converts AAS into ASA — so △ABC ≅ △DEF by AAS.

items.prompt: AAS differs from ASA in which way?
choices: AAS uses three angles; ASA uses two
In AAS the known side is NOT between the two known angles
AAS requires a right angle; ASA does not
AAS is a postulate; ASA is a theorem
items.explanation: AAS = Angle-Angle-Side, where the side is non-included (not between the two angles). ASA has the side between the angles.

items.prompt: △PQR: ∠P = 45°, ∠Q = 90°, QR = 6. △STU: ∠S = 45°, ∠T = 90°, TU = 6. Side QR is opposite ∠P; TU is opposite ∠S. Which theorem applies?
items.explanation: Two angles (∠P≅∠S, ∠Q≅∠T) and a non-included side (QR = TU, opposite the first angle) → AAS.

items.prompt: Why is AAS a theorem rather than a postulate?
choices: Because it only works for right triangles
Because it can be proved using the Triangle Angle Sum Theorem and ASA
Because it was discovered after the postulates
Because it requires more given information than ASA
hints: A theorem can be proved from other axioms and postulates.
If two angles of a triangle are known, the third is forced by the 180° sum.
Using the third-angle theorem converts AAS into ASA, which is already a postulate.

items.prompt: △ABC: ∠A = 70°, ∠C = 50°, BC = 8. △DEF: ∠D = 70°, ∠F = 50°, EF = 8. The side BC is opposite ∠A; EF is opposite ∠D. Which theorem proves congruence?
hints: Is BC between ∠A and ∠C? No — BC connects B and C, with ∠A at the opposite vertex.
Two angles and a non-included side → AAS.

items.prompt: △JKL: ∠J = 40°, JK = 9, ∠K = 60°. △MNP: ∠M = 40°, MN = 9, ∠N = 60°. Is this ASA or AAS?
choices: AAS — JK is not the included side
SAS — two angles and a side
hints: JK connects vertices J and K — which angles are at those vertices?
∠J is at vertex J and ∠K is at vertex K — both are endpoints of side JK.
JK is directly between ∠J and ∠K — this is ASA.

items.prompt: If ∠A ≅ ∠D, ∠B ≅ ∠E, and AB ≅ DE in △ABC and △DEF respectively, which postulate/theorem applies?
hints: AB connects A and B — the two vertices where the given angles are.
AB is between ∠A and ∠B → the included side → ASA.

annotations.text: BC is opposite ∠A; it is NOT between the two marked angles

testItems.prompt: △ABC: ∠A = 30°, ∠B = 110°, BC = 7. △DEF: ∠D = 30°, ∠E = 110°, EF = 7. BC is opposite ∠A; EF is opposite ∠D. Which theorem proves △ABC ≅ △DEF?
AAS is a theorem (proved), while ASA is a postulate (assumed). Why can AAS be proved?
choices: Because the third angle is forced by the 180° angle sum, converting AAS to ASA
Because AAS only applies to right triangles
Because AAS uses a shorter side

testItems.prompt: △PQR and △STU: ∠P ≅ ∠S, ∠Q ≅ ∠T, and QR ≅ TU. Is this ASA or AAS?
choices: AAS — QR is between ∠P and ∠Q, so it is included
AAS — QR connects Q and R; but the given angles are ∠P and ∠Q, and QR is not between both
ASA — because ∠Q is at one endpoint of QR
testItems.explanation: QR is between ∠Q and ∠R. Only ∠Q is given, not ∠R — so QR is non-included relative to the pair (∠P, ∠Q). This is AAS.

testItems.prompt: In the figure, AB ∥ CD and BC bisects ∠ABD and ∠ACD. Which postulate/theorem proves △ABC ≅ △DCB?
testItems.explanation: BC is shared (non-included side). ∠ABC ≅ ∠DCB (alternate interior angles, AB∥CD). The bisected angles give a second pair. AAS.

testItems.prompt: Two right triangles each have a 40° acute angle. One has a leg of 8 opposite the 40° angle; the other has a leg of 8 opposite its 40° angle. Are they congruent?
choices: Yes, by AAS — 90°, 40°, and the opposite leg match
Yes, by HL — they share a right angle

testItems.prompt: After proving △ABD ≅ △CBD by AAS, a student wants to conclude BD bisects ∠ABC. What justifies that final conclusion?
choices: The definition of an angle bisector and CPCTC
SSS applied to the original triangles
